claims.text: The initial material is a concentrated refractory high-entropy alloy in a chemically random, disordered solid-solution state.
Controlled thermal annealing can induce or enhance chemical short-range order in the alloy.
Compositional tuning can induce or enhance chemical short-range order in the alloy.
Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity relative to a random solid solution.
Specific atomic-pair correlations associated with SRO generate local lattice distortions and strain fields.
SRO-associated local lattice distortions and strain fields act as additional phonon-scattering centers.
SRO creates a heterogeneous potential landscape containing local variations in atomic mass and bond stiffness.
The heterogeneous potential landscape produced by SRO increases scattering of heat-carrying phonons.
SRO increases Umklapp phonon-scattering rates.
SRO increases point-defect phonon-scattering rates.
The SRO-induced increase in phonon scattering outweighs any increase in phonon group velocity or coherence length arising from local ordering.
Increasing the degree of SRO decreases thermal conductivity or keeps it below that of the random solid-solution baseline.
Rapid quenching or high-temperature homogenization can provide a fully random solid-solution baseline.
The proposed suppression regime requires an SRO length scale larger than the atomic spacing but smaller than the phonon mean free path.
The proposed suppression regime excludes alloys that develop long-range ordered superstructures.
The proposed suppression regime excludes alloys that undergo precipitation or phase separation.
The proposed regime applies below the Debye temperature under conditions where phonon-phonon scattering is significant.
The magnitude and possibly the direction of the SRO effect may depend strongly on alloy chemistry and the specific SRO configuration.
A statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity with increasing SRO, after excluding long-range ordering and precipitation, would falsify the suppression hypothesis.
No correlation between the SRO parameter and thermal conductivity within experimental error would falsify the predicted monotonic SRO-dependent suppression.
